audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (penultimate), not in the strict set, with a caution: 'stress not fully analysed; penult is a tendency on isolated words; shifts under affixation/in phrases (Thurston 1976:10-11, 1982:92); not lexically contrastive'. 'undetermined' is the defensible alternative if the catalog requires a stated rule.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the Thurston 1982:92 passage is verbatim in the. But the classification 'fixed-strict' (exceptionless penult, penultimate stress) is stronger than any source supports. The deciding source itself hedges ('remains to be fully analysed', 'tends to occur most frequently in penultimate position', stress 'moved.. by other morphemes', ádo ~ adó). The sole dedicated phonology, Thurston 1976 (downloaded now from MacSphere), states isolation-word accentuation 'is not predictable', lists non-penult isolation forms (/goxúp/ 'ash' final, /ándeua/ initial) alongside penult ones, says stress is not lexically distinctive, and concludes 'Probably, accentuation is morphological or syntactic; more research is required.' sources.quote: 'Three degrees of stress are recognized in Anem: primary, secondary, and non-stress ... Words spoken in isolation seem to have a characteristic accentuation which is not predictable: /kómu/ 'water', /goxúp/ 'ash', /ándeua/ 'Mt. Andewa', /asíax/ 'jungle', /aluálu/ 'bigmen'. Stress does not appear to differentiate lexical items, however. The accentuation of words in isolation often differs from their accentuation when they occur with affixes or in a sentence: /ába/ 'pig', /abáeat/ 'my pork' ... /ía/ 'fish', /iánis/ 'our (incl.) fish'. sources.note: The only dedicated phonology of Anêm (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a phonology); its stress section says isolation-word stress is 'not predictable' and gives final (goxúp) and initial (ándeua) examples, directly bearing on the 'strict' penult coding that rests on two sentences of the 1982 appendix.
